title: The Second Pair of Eyes
setting: a night editor at a newspaper

post.author: u/night_sub_eglantine
post.title: I'm the night sub-editor at a regional paper. At 01:15 I opened my own Saved page. It was full of articles I never saved, about a diagnosis and a divorce.

blocks.text: I'm the night sub-editor at the Dunmarrow Gazette. Readers who pay can keep articles to read later on a Saved page: their own list, like a pile of cuttings on a desk.

A week ago the web team made the site faster. Pages now come from computers in many towns that hand out copies close to readers: a CDN, short for content delivery network. Each of its computers is a server, a machine that answers requests.
The CDN keeps each copy, so it needn't ask us again. That kept copy is a cache.

Opening Saved takes three steps. First your web browser gets the page's frame from the CDN: the layout and a small program the page runs, a script. That frame is the shell. Then the script sends your account number to our server. Last, the server looks your list up, fresh every time.

The part that answers is a counter where one program asks another for things: an API, short for application programming interface. Before answering, it runs a rule on who may see what, an access check: if the id asked for isn't the signed-in reader's, it refuses.

The mistake: the cached shell had the first visitor's account number, their reader id, written inside: 40117. So every reader's script asked for 40117's list. The CDN never held anyone's list; only the check stood in the way. It refused everyone but 40117 with a 403, the web's number for not allowed. All week readers wrote in: Saved is broken.

At 22:40 Thorfinn, a developer, asked a program that writes code on request, a coding assistant, why Saved returned 403. Our code is JavaScript, a programming language. It called the check over-strict and suggested a change.

Here it is, shown line by line, which is called a diff. A line starting with - is removed. req.query.reader is the id the page sends; req.user.id is who is signed in; the last line fetches that list from our database, our store of records:

Every change here gets a code review: the author sends it as a pull request, a change offered for review; a second person reads and approves it; then it goes live. Chidubem approved at 22:42. Two lines that read like a bug fix. Saved worked again.
At 01:15 I opened mine. Each log line shows the time, the reader, whose list the page asked for, and the answer:

22:41  52028  40117  403, refused
22:42  the change goes live
01:15  52608  40117  40117's list, 6 articles

52608 is me. Six articles I never saved. Living with multiple sclerosis: the first year. What happens to the house in a divorce. Telling the children you are separating. Someone in Dunmarrow kept those to read in private.
My own page, full of someone else's reading.

By 06:00, 2,000 clicks on Saved since 22:42, from 1,250 readers, had all got 40117's list. The check was the only barrier between the cache's mistake and that list, and a two-minute review took it out.

blocks.label: saved_request_trace.png

diagram.aria: A trace of Eglantine's click at 01:15. Her browser opens Saved and the CDN returns the cached shell, which holds reader id 40117. The script asks the API for 40117's list. A note on the API says the access check was removed and has been live since 22:42. The API returns 40117's list of 6 articles. An outcome box says 2,000 clicks from 1,250 readers got the same list.

blocks.caption: Thorfinn traced my click. The CDN handed me the shell it had kept all week, with 40117 written inside. My page asked for 40117's list, and since 22:42 nothing said no.

blocks.text: Thorfinn wants to put the line back. Our editor asks how a change like that got through. What should we change in how we review?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Your coding assistant is a kind of AI, short for artificial intelligence: software trained on huge amounts of text, code included. Before anyone puts that line back, read what it said: if the id asked for isn't yours, refuse. For a week it refused, and nobody asked whose list all those pages were asking for. A 403 like that is a symptom, a sign of something else wrong, the way a smoke alarm is a sign of smoke. The change switched off the alarm. Now look at the review. What did Chidubem have in front of him at 22:42? Two lines and a word, over-strict. Did anything in that diff tell him what the line was for, or who would know? Your log answers the first question. The second is about your team.

replies.author: u/night_sub_eglantine
replies.text: Chidubem says he saw a small fix that made an error go away. The check was written by Anoushka, who looks after the reader accounts code. She is its code owner: the person named as answering for that code. She was asleep, and nobody asked her. Our group also has a security team, three people in the city office who look for ways into our sites. They never saw it either.

comments.author: u/four_eyes_jocasta
comments.text: One reviewer at 22:42 on a tired night is a rubber stamp. Make every change need two approvals. Two people won't both wave through a line that lets strangers read each other's lists. Pilots work this way: one flies, one cross-checks. It costs a few minutes a change, and it would have saved 1,250 readers.

comments.author: u/ban_the_bots_wolcott
comments.text: AI code is the problem; ban it from anything touching readers. These assistants don't know your paper, your readers or why any line exists, and they sound sure about everything. A person who wrote that code would have known why the check was there. Keep the robots on the weather widget and let people write the code that guards people's privacy.

reply.prompt: Thorfinn will put the check back tonight. What should the Gazette change in how it reviews code before the next fix like this? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Require two approvals on every change, so no one reviewer can wave a change through alone.
options.verdict: Two quick approvals, the same two lines
options.part2: The Gazette made every change need two approvals, and Thorfinn replayed that night on a copy of the site. Chidubem approved at 22:41 and Ilmari at 22:42. Both saw the same two lines and the same word, over-strict, and neither knew what the check was for. The change went live at 22:42: 2,000 clicks, 1,250 readers, 40117's list every time. Two people had read it, and nobody had asked what it guarded. Meanwhile every typo fix on the site now waited for a second person.
options.senior: A second approval doubles the eyes, not the knowledge. Both reviewers read the same diff, which showed what was removed and not why it was there, so the same blind spot is approved twice. Approvals count people; this change needed the right person and the right question. Use two approvals where the risk justifies it, and send security-sensitive code to someone who knows what it protects.

options.text: Ban coding-assistant suggestions in code that touches readers, so only people write it.
options.verdict: The same two lines, by hand
options.part2: The Gazette banned coding-assistant suggestions in any code that touches readers. Thorfinn replayed the night writing the change himself. He saw what the assistant had seen: a 403, and the line that sent it. He wrote the same two lines. Chidubem approved at 22:42: two lines that read like a bug fix. 2,000 clicks, 1,250 readers, 40117's list. Who typed the line made no difference to the review.
options.senior: The assistant made a plausible suggestion from what it could see, which is what a person in a hurry does too. Banning the tool removes one source of fluent code, not the gap in review. Review AI-written code the way you would a confident new colleague's: every line, and the reason behind anything removed. The author is not the control; the review is.

options.text: Send every change to the site through the security team for review before it goes live.
options.verdict: Trade-off: safe, slow, and blind to the cause
options.part2: Every change to the site went through the security team. Replayed, Thorfinn's change joined their queue behind 11 others, and nothing shipped that night. Saved stayed broken: 2,120 clicks, every one refused, and nobody saw a stranger's list. At 09:30 the team rejected it because it removed an access check. Nobody asked why the check had been refusing all week, so 40117's id stayed in the cached shell. By 06:00, 12 changes had been waiting, a typo fix in a headline among them.
options.senior: A security review catches a removed access check, and that matters. But sending every change through one small team turns it into a queue: typo fixes wait beside access checks, and the team reviews without knowing the code, so it blocks the symptom and misses the cause. Keep security reviewers for the riskiest changes and for setting the rules, and let ownership put the right reviewer on each sensitive path.

options.text: Make changes to access checks need their owner's review, saying what each check guards.
options.part2: The Gazette named an owner for every access check: Anoushka for the reader accounts code. A change to one now waits for her, and the review asks what the check guards. Replayed, Thorfinn's change waited all night. Saved stayed broken: 2,120 clicks refused, none leaked. At 08:10 Anoushka answered: it stops one reader seeing another reader's list, so a 403 means a page is asking for someone else's. She rejected the change and found 40117 written into the cached shell. The web team made the script ask for the signed-in reader's own list, with no id in the shell, and the check stayed. Every other change still needs one approval.
options.senior: Put the right person, not more people, on the code that protects data. An owner knows why a check exists, and asking what it guards makes the reason part of the review. A removed safety check is a change to read twice: the error it causes is usually a symptom pointing at the real bug. The cost is that sensitive changes wait for one person, so name a deputy, and back the owner with a test that asks for another reader's list and expects a 403.

sim.title: Run Saved through the night
sim.lede: You're Eglantine, replaying Saved from 22:00. A week ago the CDN cached the Saved page's shell with reader 40117's id inside, so every page asks the API for 40117's list. The given data: 120 clicks on Saved between 22:00 and 22:41, then 2,000 between 22:42 and 06:00 from 1,250 readers; 40117 doesn't open Saved that night. The access check refuses any page that asks for another reader's list, with a 403. At 22:40 Thorfinn's two-line change, which removes the check, goes to review. One approval or two lets it go live at 22:42. The security team keeps it in their queue with 11 others and rejects it at 09:30. The code owner, Anoushka, is asked what the check guards, and answers at 08:10. With the cache fixed, the shell holds no id and each page asks for its own reader's list. Pick the check, the cache, the review rule and who wrote the two lines, then press Run the night.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press Run the night as it happened: 120 refused before 22:42, then 2,000 clicks get 40117's list and 1,250 readers see another reader's articles. Switch to two approvals, then to Thorfinn writing the lines by hand: the same count. Try the security team and the code owner: Saved stays broken all night, 2,120 refused, but read who finds the cause. Then fix the cache, with the check kept and with it removed.

explain.oneLine: Nothing on the server misbehaved. A cached shell made every page ask for one reader's list, the access check refused, and a two-line change that looked like a bug fix removed the only barrier. The review read the lines, not what they guarded.

steps.title: One shell, one id, every reader.
steps.text: Opening Saved is a process of three steps. First the browser gets the shell from the CDN; since the caching change, that is one kept copy for everyone, and what went wrong here is that the copy had reader 40117's id written into it. Then the script sends that id to the API, so every page asked for 40117's list. Last, the API runs its access check and looks the list up fresh in the database. The CDN never held anyone's list. The only thing between the cache's mistake and a leak was the check in step three.

steps.title: The 403s were the check doing its job.
steps.text: A 403 means the server understood the request and refused it. For a week it refused every reader but 40117, and readers called Saved broken. The error was a symptom: the real question was why pages were asking for someone else's list. The assistant was asked a narrower question, why does Saved return 403, and gave the narrow answer: remove the line that sends it. The bug was in the cache all along.

steps.title: What a review is for.
steps.text: A code review is a process too. First the author sends a small change with a note on why. Then a reviewer reads every line and asks: is it correct, is there a test that would fail if it broke, and if a line is removed, why was it there? Then they approve or ask for changes. What can go wrong: a change that looks small and reads like a fix gets approved by someone who doesn't know the code. Small changes help, because a reviewer can hold all of them in mind; a checklist helps, because it asks the dull questions every time. Code that guards data, such as access checks, needs the closest read.

steps.title: Read AI-written code like a confident new colleague's.
steps.text: A coding assistant writes fluent, plausible code with no doubt in its voice. It sees only what it is shown: here, a 403 and the line that sends it. That makes it like a confident new colleague: usually right, sometimes wrong in exactly the line that matters, and never likely to say so. Banning it wouldn't help, because Thorfinn, seeing the same thing, would have written the same two lines. Review its work as you would any author's: every line, the reason behind every removal, and the person who submits it answers for it.

steps.title: Give sensitive code an owner, and ask what it guards.
steps.text: A code owner is the person named for a part of the code. The process: first the files that hold access checks are listed with their owner, in a CODEOWNERS file on many code-hosting sites. Then any change to those files asks the owner for review automatically, and it can't go live without their approval. Then the review asks one question in writing: what does this check guard? What can go wrong: the owner is away, so the change waits; or the access code lives in a file nobody listed. Anoushka's answer, it stops one reader seeing another's list, turns a 403 from a nuisance into a clue.

diagram.aria: The fix. A reader's browser gets the shell from the CDN; the shell now holds no reader id and is the same for everyone. The browser asks the Saved API for my list. The API works out who is signed in, keeps its access check, and reads that reader's list from the Saved lists database. A note under the API says the check's owner is Anoushka and that every change to it must say what it guards.

notes.text: owner: Anoushka; changes say what it guards

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the next change. The shell the CDN keeps holds no reader id, so every page asks for the signed-in reader's own list. The access check stays, and its owner reviews any change to it, starting with what it guards.

fix.title: The fix: owners for access checks, a written reason, and the cache mended
fix.text: Put the line back tonight. Then name an owner for every access check, Anoushka for the reader accounts code, and make a change to those files wait for the owner's approval. Add one question to the review template: what does this check guard, and why is it safe to change? Add a test that asks the API for another reader's list and expects a 403, so the check can't be removed quietly. Then fix the real bug: take the reader id out of the cached shell, and have the API use the signed-in reader for Saved. Everything else keeps one approval, and changes stay small enough to read in one sitting.

limits: An owner is one person. When Anoushka is asleep or away, sensitive changes wait, as Thorfinn's did all night, so the rule needs a named deputy, and an emergency route that is reviewed afterwards.

The owner still sees only the diff. If the change doesn't say why it removes or changes a check, the owner has to ask, so the question about what the check guards belongs in the review template, not in anyone's memory.

Review is people reading, and people miss things, as Heartbleed's review did. A test that asks for another reader's list and expects a 403 keeps guarding the check on nights when nobody reads closely.

head: Review rule
Good
Bad
rows: Fast. Small fixes go out in minutes.
One tired reader of two fluent lines. 1,250 readers saw another's list.
Both see the same diff and the same blind spot. Every typo fix waits for two.
Fewer fluent changes from a tool that can't see the whole system.
A person writes the same two lines. The gap was in review, not the author.
The security team reviews every change
A removed access check is caught.
A queue for every change, reviewed without context. The cause stays hidden.
Code owner for access checks, asked what each guards
The person who knows why the check exists reads the change. The 403 becomes a clue.
Sensitive changes wait for one person. Covers only the code listed.

explain.seniorTake: Review is for the reason behind the change, not the lines alone. Keep changes small, read every line, and treat a removed check or test as the change to read twice: the error it silences is usually a symptom of the real bug. Send security-sensitive code to the person who knows what it protects, and make them say it in writing. Review code an assistant wrote as you would a confident new colleague's: fluent, plausible and sometimes wrong in the one line that matters, with the person who submits it answering for it. Then back every review with a test, because people miss things and tests don't get tired.

realWorld.title: Heartbleed, 2014: the CVE record
realWorld.text: The National Vulnerability Database describes CVE-2014-0160 this way: "The (1) TLS and (2) DTLS implementations in OpenSSL 1.0.1 before 1.0.1g do not properly handle Heartbeat Extension packets, which allows remote attackers to obtain sensitive information from process memory via crafted packets that trigger a buffer over-read, as demonstrated by reading private keys, related to d1_both.c and t1_lib.c, aka the Heartbleed bug."

realWorld.title: The OpenSSL advisory, 7 April 2014
realWorld.text: OpenSSL's security advisory, under the heading TLS heartbeat read overrun (CVE-2014-0160), says: "A missing bounds check in the handling of the TLS heartbeat extension can be used to reveal up to 64k of memory to a connected client or server." It told users to upgrade to OpenSSL 1.0.1g. One missing check, like the Gazette's one removed check.

realWorld.title: It had been reviewed
realWorld.text: The commit that added heartbeat support to OpenSSL, the change that, by most accounts, brought in the missing check, records a review in its message, on a line that begins "Reviewed by:". Review happened, and the one line that mattered still went through.

realWorld.title: Google: what to look for in a code review
realWorld.text: Google's published engineering practices tell reviewers: "In the general case, look at every line of code that you have been assigned to review." If a reviewer can't read it all, "you should at least be sure that you understand what all the code is doing." On tests they ask: "Will the tests actually fail when the code is broken?"

realWorld.title: Code owners, as a code-hosting site builds them
realWorld.text: GitHub's documentation says: "You can use a CODEOWNERS file to define individuals or teams that are responsible for code in a repository." And: "Code owners are automatically requested for review when someone opens a pull request that modifies code that they own." Repository admins can also require a code owner's approval before a change is merged.

realWorld.title: The other half: LATENT, The Apprentice That Writes Code
realWorld.text: This case reviews a change from the reviewer's chair; LATENT's The Apprentice That Writes Code takes the coding agent's side of the same work. Google's line holds for both: look at every line you have been assigned to review.

asked: What do you look for in a code review?
How do you review code an AI wrote?
How do you protect security-sensitive code paths?
interview.answer: First, I read the description and ask what the change is for, then read every line. I look for correctness, including the odd cases; for tests that would fail if the code broke; and for anything removed, because a deleted check or test needs a reason, and the error it silences is often a symptom of a different bug. I ask for small changes, since I can't review four hundred lines well, and I use a short checklist for the dull questions. For code an AI wrote, I review it as I would a confident new colleague's: it is fluent and plausible, it saw only what it was shown, and it can be wrong in exactly the line that matters. The person who submits it answers for every line, and I don't relax because it reads well. For security-sensitive paths such as access checks, I give them owners, so a change there can't merge without the person who knows what it protects, and the change must say what the check guards. I back that with tests, for example one that asks for another user's data and expects a 403, and keep a security team for the riskiest changes and for setting the rules, not as a queue for every typo fix.

terms.def: A newspaper editor who checks stories for mistakes, cuts them to fit and writes headlines before they print. Eglantine works the night shift.
The Gazette website's list of articles a reader has kept to read later. Each reader's should show only their own.
Short for content delivery network: servers in many towns that keep copies of a site's pages close to readers, so each page arrives faster.
A machine, and the program on it, that waits for requests and answers them, like a clerk behind a counter.
A kept copy of an answer, so nobody has to ask again, like a note by the phone. Fast, but everyone who gets the copy gets the same thing.
The app you use to visit websites, such as Chrome, Firefox or Safari.
The part of a web page that is the same for everyone: its layout and its script. The Saved list is fetched afterwards. The Gazette's cached shell wrongly held one reader's id.
A small program a web page runs in your browser. The Saved page's script asks the API for a reader's list.
The number on a reader's account. 40117 was written into the cached shell; 52608 is Eglantine.
Short for application programming interface: a counter where one program asks another for something, with a fixed form for asking. The Saved API hands out reading lists.
Code that decides who may see or change what, and refuses everyone else. The Saved API's check refused any page asking for a list that wasn't the signed-in reader's.
The reader the server knows is using the page, because they logged in. In the code, req.user.id.
The web's status number for refused: the server understood the request and won't allow it. Signing in again won't help.
A person who writes and changes the code a website runs on. Thorfinn is one of the Gazette's.
A program, built on an AI language model, that writes or changes code when you describe what you want. It sounds sure whether it is right or not.
Short for artificial intelligence: here, software trained on huge amounts of text, code included, that writes fluent answers. Coding assistants are built on it.
A programming language, first made for web pages and now also run on servers through a tool called Node.js. The Gazette's Saved API is written in it.
A change shown line by line: lines starting with - are removed, + added, the rest unchanged. Thorfinn's removed one line.
A program that stores records so other programs can find and change them. The Gazette's holds every reader's saved list.
A second person reading a change to the code before it goes live, looking for mistakes and asking why each part is there.
A change offered for review before it joins the main code. Reviewers comment, approve or ask for changes; then it is merged.
A reviewer's yes to a change, after which it can be merged and go live. Chidubem's came two minutes after Thorfinn asked.
A change that corrects code that does the wrong thing. Thorfinn's change looked like one and was a bug in itself.
A sign of a problem rather than the problem itself, like a smoke alarm going off. The 403s were a symptom; the cached id was the cause.
The person or team named as answering for a part of the code. A change to it waits for their review. Anoushka owns the reader accounts code.
A file in a code store, used by GitHub and similar sites, that lists which people own which files, so they are asked to review changes to them.
A group whose job is finding ways into a company's systems before attackers do. The Gazette's group has three people in its city office.
A short list of questions a reviewer answers for every change, such as: does any line remove a check or a test, and why?
A small program that runs part of the code with a known input and checks the answer, such as asking for another reader's list and expecting a 403.
A 2014 bug in OpenSSL: a missing bounds check let anyone connected ask for up to 64k of a server's memory, which could hold private keys.
Free code that many websites use to encrypt their connections. Heartbleed was a bug in its heartbeat handling.
Short for Transport Layer Security: the way a browser and a server encrypt their conversation, the S in HTTPS. DTLS is a version for another kind of traffic.
A small are-you-there message one side of a TLS connection sends, which the other side echoes back.
A check that a number, such as a length someone sends, stays within what is really there before the code uses it.
Reading past the end of the memory meant to be read, so the program hands out whatever happens to lie next to it.
Where a running program keeps what it is working on. A server's can hold secrets such as its private keys.
The secret half of a key pair that proves a server is who it says it is. Anyone who has it can pretend to be that server.
Short for Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: a public list that gives each known security bug a number, such as CVE-2014-0160.
One saved change to a project's code, with a message saying what it does and, often, who reviewed it.

atWork: Look for an access check that someone removed or loosened in a tidy-up because it was "unnecessary" or "too strict". A common pattern: a check refuses something for a reason nobody remembers, a change removes it to make an error go away, and the error was a clue to a different bug. Read-only access to the code store is enough. Search recent merged changes for removed lines that return 401, 403 or 404, or that compare a requested id with the signed-in user's. For each, read the review: did anyone ask what the check guarded? Then look at who owns your access-check code: is there a CODEOWNERS file, does it list those paths, and does the branch require the owner's approval? Finally, look for a test that asks for another user's data and expects a refusal. If your company is working towards ISO/IEC 27001:2022, controls A.8.25 (secure development life cycle) and A.8.32 (change management) cover this, and owner review of access-control changes, with the reason recorded, is evidence for both. If it is pursuing SOC 2, criterion CC8.1 covers authorising and approving changes. If you hold EU residents' personal data, GDPR Article 32 asks for appropriate technical and organisational security measures, and a reading list like 40117's is personal data.

recall.prompt: You are the second reviewer on a teammate's pull request, mostly written by a coding assistant. It deletes one line from the code that serves invoices: if (invoice.accountId !== req.user.accountId) return res.sendStatus(404). The description says it fixes 404 errors customers reported since last week's change to links in emails. It is three lines, and one person has already approved. What do you do?

keyIdeas.idea: The deleted line is an access check; ask what it guards before it goes
The 404s are a symptom: find why customers' requests ask for invoices that aren't theirs (the email links) and fix that cause
Bring in the owner of that code and add a test that another account is still refused

recall.model: I'd block it. The deleted line is an access check: it refuses anyone asking for an invoice on another account, and it must not go just because it raises errors. Those 404s are a symptom; since last week's change, the email links probably carry the wrong id, so find out why the requests ask for invoices that aren't the customer's and fix that, the real cause. I'd ask the code owner of the billing code to review, and add a test that asks for an invoice on another account and expects a 404, so the check can't be removed quietly. A fluent three-line diff, from an assistant or a person, gets the same read: every line, and why anything removed was there.

recall.prompt: OpenSSL's advisory of 7 April 2014 described the bug later called Heartbleed. What did it say the bug was?
options: A missing bounds check that could reveal up to 64k of memory to a connected client or server
A weak random number generator that made private keys easy to guess
An expired certificate that browsers kept trusting for months
A login check that let anyone in with an empty password
recall.why: The advisory says a missing bounds check in the handling of the TLS heartbeat extension can be used to reveal up to 64k of memory to a connected client or server. The change that brought it in had been through review, and still nobody noticed the missing check.

recall.prompt: Your team lead says code from the coding assistant is either fine or obviously broken, so a quick glance is enough, and plans to let it send pull requests to the payments service. What do you tell them?

keyIdeas.idea: Assistant code is fluent and plausible, and its mistakes are quiet, in the line that matters
Review it like a confident new colleague's work: every line, and the reason behind each removal
Keep its changes small, send sensitive code to its owner, and back review with tests

recall.model: Its mistakes are rarely obvious. Assistant code is fluent and plausible, and it is written from what the assistant was shown, so when it is wrong it is wrong quietly, often in the one line that matters, like a removed check. Review it like a confident new colleague's work: read every line, ask why anything was removed, and hold the person who submits it to account for it. Keep its pull requests to small changes so they can be read properly, send sensitive code such as payments and access checks to the code owner, and back the review with tests that would fail if the code broke.

recall.prompt: In the Gazette's replay with two approvals, Chidubem approved at 22:41 and Ilmari at 22:42, and 1,250 readers still saw 40117's list. Why didn't the second approval help?
options: Ilmari approved too quickly; a minimum review time would have caught it
Both read the same two lines, and neither knew what the check guarded
Two approvals only work when one reviewer is from the security team
The change was written by a coding assistant, which reviewers can't judge
recall.why: Both reviewers saw the same diff, which shows what was removed but not why it was there, and neither knew the code. More people with the same view approve the same blind spot. The change needed the person who knew what the check guarded, its owner.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. Access checks now need Anoushka's review, and Saved has stayed private. Last week Thorfinn asked the coding assistant to tidy the reader accounts code. It came back as one pull request of 412 lines across 38 files. Anoushka reviewed the one file she owns, where the checks live, and it was fine. Chidubem approved the other 37 files in nine minutes. Among them was a new download button that sends a reader's saved articles as a file. It takes the reader id from the address, as the old line did, and nothing refuses a stranger's id. On Sunday a reader emailed us a file of saved articles that weren't hers.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. How did this get past the owner rule, and what should the Gazette change?

keyIdeas.idea: The pull request was far too big to review line by line; split work into small changes
The owner rule covers only listed files; the new download code handed out lists from a file nobody owned
Make every route that returns reader data go through one shared check, and test it by asking for another reader's list

coldCase.model: The owner rule only covers the files it lists. The download button was new code in a file nobody owned, so it got an ordinary review, and its missing check went through like the old one. And 412 lines in 38 files is too big to read line by line in nine minutes; ask for smaller changes, one purpose each, and refuse tidy-ups that mix in new features. Then move the decision into one shared check, middleware that every route returning reader data must pass, that uses the signed-in reader and owned by Anoushka, so a new route can't forget it. Add a test for every such route that asks for another reader's list and expects a 403, and list any new file that hands out reader data under her ownership.
